column2: The two men reached Shanghai that same day and took rooms at Yuji Silk Warehouse. Gu Yingchun hurried over when he heard they had arrived. He looked slightly embarrassed on seeing Hu Xueyan, who naturally would not mention the Seventh Lady in such circumstances. First he listened to Gu's account of the Shanghai market. Silk prices had risen. With Pang Er's support, everyone was holding together and waiting for a satisfactory price. But the foreigners, too, seemed formidable. By every means they could devise, they went inland to buy silk themselves, brought it by roundabout routes to Shanghai, and assembled it for shipment overseas. “This cannot last,” Gu said excitedly. “First, it's troublesome; second, it costs a good deal; third, once the Liangjiang governor-general's yamen has issued its proclamation, it must uphold its authority. Naturally, troops will be stationed at the checkpoints to inspect shipments and prevent anyone forcing a passage. In my view, the foreigners will soon have to come to terms. You've arrived at exactly the right time.”

The report pleased Hu. Yet he had so much to do on this journey that he must put his business in order of urgency and attend to it item by item. His first question concerned He Guiqing's whereabouts. “That I don't know,” Gu said. “The provincial education commissioner has to visit the prefectures and departments to conduct the regular examinations of licentiates. I don't know where he is just now, but we can certainly find out. Leave that to me.” “It isn't only finding him. There's an important letter to be delivered by a special messenger.” “That can be arranged too. Give me the letter.” With this settled, they turned to Zhejiang's gun purchase. Since receiving Hu's letter, Gu had made preliminary inquiries, but the foreign merchant had gone to Ningbo and would not return to Shanghai for several days. They could only wait.

The two most urgent matters discussed, it was time to speak of the Seventh Lady. Hu had agreed with You Laowu on the journey that You must withdraw at this point. At a glance from Hu, he rose, saying that he had a friend to see. “Brother Five,” Gu said, “I'm giving Hu a welcome dinner. Come and have foreign food with us.” “What's so good about foreign food? All those knives and forks—I can't be bothered. You go.” As his figure disappeared, Hu smiled. “You've kept me nicely in the dark, Old Gu!” At this, Gu became agitated. “You mean Seventh Sister? If I'd deliberately concealed it, I wouldn't deserve to be called your friend. If even you won't understand me, I'll have nowhere left to turn!” “Don't get excited. Tell me slowly, and we'll think of something together. I refuse to believe I can't make this match.” These words greatly reassured Gu. “I was afraid I couldn't explain it properly in a letter, and I knew you'd be coming soon, so I decided to say nothing. I was waiting for you to act as my strategist. You don't know how anxious I am, with the affair in this state. It's just like...” He swallowed and could not finish. “Like what? Give me an image, and I'll understand where your difficulty lies.” “Like being trapped behind a wall raised by ghosts. I can't understand how I suddenly found myself in this predicament.”

Hu laughed. “Wine overcomes restraint, and there you were with someone you'd always liked. The raw rice has gone into the pot, yet you can't cook it into a proper meal. No wonder you're anxious!” “Exactly!” Gu clapped his hands. “A perfect comparison. To tell you honestly, when I go to her, my eyes feast and my stomach hungers, but nothing reaches my mouth—all because the rice cannot be cooked!” “What? You really haven't been intimate with Seventh Sister since that night?” Hu remembered You's account: she had told her brother that Gu had never spent a night at her place. Now Gu himself said much the same, and Hu could not help doubting it. He knew men's habits. The Seventh Lady, moreover, was bold, unconventional and careless of restraint. After that night's happy encounter, why had the lovers not come together again? It hardly seemed reasonable. He and Gu were close enough to discuss anything. To speak of bedroom matters might be indiscreet, but given the Seventh Lady's unusual circumstances, it was hardly an affront to her. He smiled. “Dry wood and a blazing fire, yet they burned only once? That's rather curious.”

“Once I explain, you won't think it curious. There are two reasons. First, since I intend to marry her formally as my wife, I ought to show her respect. That night was a different matter—as you said, wine overcame restraint. Second, the marriage still faces obstacles, and no one can predict the outcome. If it fails, I'd have wronged both her and Brother Five, quite apart from what my conscience would say. People who didn't know the circumstances would accuse me of seducing and abandoning her. The foreign settlement is full of gossips. With a reputation like that, who knows what a villain they'd make of me!” Hu's respect rose at these words. His smile disappeared. “Old Gu, with intentions like yours, this marriage cannot fail. It's still early. I'll go and see Seventh Sister first.” Gu found this profoundly comforting.

After a moment's thought, Gu answered, “Then let's have dinner at her place. There's still some food at home today.” His tone made it clear that he and the Seventh Lady were already like husband and wife, lacking only the fulfilment of their shared dream. Their affection was plainly strong. Here were two people perfectly suited to one another, a match that ought to follow naturally, and that meddling Cheng Yaojin had to appear, brandishing clan rules. Infuriating! Hu felt a surge of defiance. Striking his chest, he declared, “Don't worry, Old Gu. Leave that old clan head to me.” “Wait, Hu!” Gu said nervously. “He's a great-uncle of mine, and he taught my late father. You mustn't act rashly. Tell me, how do you propose to ‘deal with’ him?” “‘Deal with’ may sound rather unpleasant. I'm not trying to make him lose face. I'm trying to win his consent.” “That's right.” Gu brightened. “Tell me quickly, so I can share the pleasure.” “It isn't time for pleasure yet, only reassurance. We must see how things work out. I do have a plan, but I must speak to Seventh Sister first.” “When? Should I keep out of the way?” “That would be best.” “Then I'll take you there and go to a foreign provision shop to buy some game. You can talk while I'm out.”

Having agreed, Gu hired a “Hengsimei” carriage and took Hu to the Seventh Lady's lodgings in Qipan Street. She was overjoyed to see him. “Little Uncle, after Gu left last night, I cast the dominoes and divined that an honoured helper would come today. Sure enough, here you are! A bodhisattva come to save my life!” Then she glanced at Gu. “It's that unfortunate surname of theirs. We had to come up against a stubborn old Gu—a hidebound old stick! He's made me so angry my stomach's nearly acting up.” “Don't be angry. So long as you'll listen to me, I guarantee you'll be called Gu yourself.” At this, Gu rose and, following their agreed plan, excused himself to buy game at the foreign provision shop. Once he had gone, her manner changed. Her pride made her pretend indifference in front of Gu. Alone with Hu, however, she behaved as though she had truly found an uncle of her own. Her face was full of hurt and distress. Compared with her usual bold, carefree manner, it scarcely seemed the same person. “Little Uncle,” she said, her voice close to tears, “what am I to do, left hanging like this? All my life I've tried to hold my head high, and now I've landed myself in something I can't hold my head high about. That's why I seldom go back to Songjiang. I really can't face people. You must find some way to help me.” “Don't worry. There must be a way.” Hu asked carefully, “But I must understand. Is it that you love each other too much to part, or that your pride is involved?” “Both. When it comes to reputation, it's always the woman who suffers. Ah, I have myself to blame. I tried a fancy trick with a spear and wounded myself.”

Hu was exceptionally good at reading a person's tone. At once he sensed more behind her words. “What trick did you play?” Her expression became extraordinary: amusement, pride, shame and regret mingled in it. Even Hu, so practised at reading faces, could not guess what she had in mind. “Well?” he deliberately provoked her. “If you can't bring yourself to say it, never mind.” “I can say it. I'm only afraid... afraid you won't believe me.” “Leave that to me. Not to boast, but whatever else I can't do, I can tell when people speak the truth or lie, how much of the truth they tell and how far their falsehood goes. None of that escapes me.” “I believe that.” Her expression changed again, becoming earnest. “You're the only person I could tell. I wouldn't even tell Fifth Sister-in-Law. She would be sure to blame me. But first, Little Uncle, what are people saying about me?” “People? What people? I've heard only what Brother Five told me.” “What did he say?” How could Hu repeat such words as ‘wine overcomes restraint’? After considering, he answered, “Brother Five said Gu wasn't to blame.” Though discreetly phrased, the meaning was plain to her. “Naturally, the blame is mine! As though I'd made myself cheap. Heaven is my witness—nothing of the sort happened!” “What didn't happen?” Hu asked in astonishment.

Even a woman as free-spoken as the Seventh Lady blushed at that question. Composing her face and lowering her eyes, she replied, “You're my elder, Little Uncle, so there's no harm in telling you. To this day, Gu has never touched my body.” “So that's it!” Hu was more puzzled than ever. “Then where did ‘that affair’ come from?” “I made him believe he'd done it.” “Why?” “Why?” Now she raised her face. “Surely even that worldly, ingenious heart of yours can understand!” A little thought made it plain. She must have been afraid Gu would change his mind, deliberately made him drunk, and claimed that they had been intimate. His sense of duty and conscience would then oblige him to marry her. It was a stratagem Hu would never have dreamed of. How unlike other women she was showed fully in this device. She had gone to extraordinary lengths, and he could not help admiring the courage with which she had burned her boats. Yet their friendship was close; he truly regarded her as his own younger sister. More than admiration, he felt disapproval. “What an idea to have! Never mind Fifth Sister-in-Law—I blame you too. Gu has a conscience. What he told me showed him to be a true gentleman. But suppose he'd refused to shoulder the responsibility? Wouldn't you have got the reputation before getting the shoes, as they say? A respectable woman, with a story like that going about! You may not care, but you've made Brother Five lose face whenever he goes out. Think about it. Was it worth it?”

His words filled her with regret and agitation. “Oh dear!” She wrung her hands and drew in her breath. “You've reminded me, Little Uncle. I never thought I might make Brother Five lose face. What... what am I to do?” Hu had never seen her so anxious. He felt deeply sorry for her and was about to comfort her when another thought occurred to him. She feared neither heaven nor earth and would listen to no one. Here was a rare chance to teach her a lesson. He made his face sterner. “Seventh Sister,” he said, his voice quiet but cold, “you think only of pleasing yourself, never of other people. By damaging your own honour like this, you damage the You family's name. Your parents must grieve for it in their graves. You really must change your ways.” Mention of her parents stung her conscience still more. Her face flushed; tears trembled in her eyes. She could only look at him, pleading for understanding and help. Hu's voice softened into earnestness. “A woman is still a woman. Her ability must show in the right sphere. If she can do what a man by his nature cannot, that is real ability. If you're capable in exactly the way a man is, only a useless husband will let your strengths shine. Otherwise, it can never end well. Why? A husband with spirit may put up with almost anything, but never with a wife humiliating him in public.”

The Seventh Lady said nothing. It was not that she had no answer, but everyone she met praised her ability. They either called her a woman with a man's courage or said she was more useful than a man. This was the first time she had heard anything like Hu's words, and she needed to consider them carefully. The more she did, the more they resembled an olive: sour and astringent at first, increasingly sweet in the aftertaste. For years she had had the upper hand in public life, but only she knew her private suffering as a woman. Alone beside a solitary lamp, with cold bedding and an empty place beside her pillow, all those ringing cries of “Seventh Sister! Seventh Sister!” were useless. What she longed for was a husband and children. She would willingly cook and wash; at least her toil would have a purpose. “There are men and women just as heaven and earth have yin and yang, and all things have firmness and softness. If women were the same as men, there'd be yang without yin, firmness without softness. What sort of world would that be? And if both husband and wife have forceful, unyielding temperaments, how can they live in harmony? Seventh Sister, am I right?” Directly asked, she could no longer remain silent. “Yes. I've never heard this before. If someone had said it earlier, I wouldn't have developed such a temper.” “It's still not too late to change,” Hu replied at once. “Mountains and rivers are easier to alter than a person's nature.” She paused. “I'll try.” “Good. If you're determined and want to show what you can do, you can change. If you can't...” He deliberately stopped. Naturally, she asked, “What if I can't?” “Then, honestly, you'd better not marry Gu. Even if you did, your temperaments wouldn't agree.”

She thought this went too far, but could hardly argue and gave no answer. “You don't believe me, do you?” “It isn't that,” she hastened to say. “Gu comes often and spends plenty of time here. He's never said anything.” “I know,” Hu replied calmly. “For one thing, you're both being polite to each other at present. For another, men and women think differently before and after marriage. What Gu values in you is your good heart and frank, generous spirit. Don't turn your strengths into weaknesses. Turn your weaknesses into strengths.” This won her admiration. “There's wisdom in those words, Little Uncle. I'll listen.” “That's right. If you'll listen, naturally I'll concern myself with your affairs. Otherwise, why make a match only to be cursed for it?” He continued, “First tell me, Seventh Sister: would you be willing to change your surname?” Her eyes widened. “Change it? To what? Why?” “It certainly wouldn't disgrace you. Oh!” Something occurred to him, and he asked urgently, “There's another important question. Has the old Gu clan head ever seen you?” “No. I've never met anyone from their family.” “Then we're certain to succeed. We'll use my plan to carry you safely past him without his knowing.”

Hu's plan was to have Wang Youling acknowledge the Seventh Lady as his sister. They would not say that the relationship was adoptive, so she must take the surname Wang. Gu would propose marriage to the Wang family; the bride's family would consent, and Wang himself would present the document giving her birth details. Out of respect for a prefect, the old clan head would find it difficult to refuse even if he learned the truth. Since he had never met her, however, deceiving him would be easy. The Seventh Lady could scarcely stop smiling. “Little Uncle, you're a real Zhuge Liang! Even if that old Gu fellow were Cao Cao, he'd still be beaten by you. But...” Her brows drew together slightly, and her smile faded. “What is Prefect Wang's position, and what is mine? How could I presume to claim such a connection?” “Don't concern yourself with that. Leave it to me.” “There's also Brother Five. I don't know what he'll think.” “If it's for your good, there's no reason for him to refuse. Leave that to me too.” She considered the plan from beginning to end and could find no obstacle. Only one concern remained: could she pass for the lady of a prefect's family? This brought a fresh resolve. “I really will change,” she said. “I must look like a daughter of an official household.” “Exactly. Now you're in earnest.”

Just then, the rumble of a carriage approached. She knew the sound. “Gu's back!” Lifting the curtain, she looked out. Hu rose to look too. Two figures appeared in the dusk, dimly recognizable as Gu and You. When they came upstairs, he saw that he was right. As Gu handed her a large parcel of smoked quail and other game, he could not help studying her face. Her expression was open and relaxed; the underlying gloom of so many days had vanished. “Well? What good idea has Hu found?” Even You brightened at the question, looking eagerly from Hu to his sister. She was moved. She had thought he deliberately neglected her troubles and rarely visited because he meant to show his displeasure. She had resented him deeply. Only now did she see how much he cared. She became more restrained and considerate. “Let Little Uncle tell you. We must ask Brother Five about this.” With that, she went lightly downstairs to the kitchen. Hu explained his plan. Gu was delighted; You remained more composed. His objection was the same as his sister's had been. “I know your friendship with Prefect Wang. One word from you is certain to settle it. But we must take a look in the mirror. Even if we claim such a grand connection and he doesn't disdain us, other people will gossip.” “Brother Five, I can't admire that remark,” Hu said frankly. “Are you the sort of man who fears what others say?” You looked ashamed. “Among ourselves, I'll tell the truth. These last two years, I really have become rather afraid of trouble. The proverb is right: ‘For your first three years abroad, you can go anywhere under heaven; after another three, you can scarcely take a step.’ I often think of that now.”

Hu and Gu remained silent. They did not know whether You had something particular in mind and thought it best to say nothing. “Enough of that. We'll follow Little Uncle's plan. Tell me what preparations courtesy requires of me.” “That's a small matter. First, we must plan for Gu. To carry this off, we must treat the previous marriage proposal as having failed and begin afresh with a daughter of the Wang family. Only then will it look convincing.” “Exactly.” You added solemnly, “One thing: please tell A’qi she must stop living here. She must go back to Songjiang first.” This reminded Hu of something. He smiled at Gu. “Forgive me. I must tell Brother Five a rather amusing story.” If it was amusing, why not let everyone hear it? Why tell it behind someone's back? Evidently it concerned Gu himself. He was bewildered, and You was puzzled too. But when Hu told You what his sister had confessed, he really did laugh, loudly. A small part was amusement; most was joy. Whatever her flightiness or recklessness, his sister had, after all, remained chaste. Gu could contain himself no longer. He came over. “What's so funny? Tell me, so I can laugh too.” Neither answered. Instead, they exchanged a glance, silently consulting each other. “He ought to be told,” You said firmly. Naturally, it fell to Hu to do the telling. He drew Gu aside and revealed the Seventh Lady's secret.

“No wonder!” Gu exclaimed, immensely relieved. A mystery he had carried for days, unable to discuss it with anyone, was solved. When he had awoken towards dawn that night, he had found her sitting alone by the lamp in a light lined jacket, faint traces of tears beneath her eyes. She had told him that she had given him everything and made him swear before the lamp never to change his heart. Feeling that he had wronged her, he had done whatever she asked. Yet sometimes, in quiet reflection, he could recall nothing of that enchanting scene—her soft, warm, fragrant body in his arms—still less the rapture itself. To have passed one of life's rarest nights so muddled and unaware seemed more regrettable than Pigsy swallowing the ginseng fruit without tasting it. Only now did he learn that ‘Pigsy’ had been deceived. But being deceived was better than not being deceived. Until now, his determination to marry no one but the Seventh Lady had chiefly rested on duty. Now his feelings returned to those of their first meeting: all his attention fixed upon her, his whole heart devoted to her. He bowed deeply to Hu again. “You must bring this about—as quickly as possible!” “Good things meet many obstacles. Be patient.” Hu rubbed his stomach. “I'm really hungry.”

You and Gu felt the same. What elaborate dish was their hostess making that kept dinner so long? They were about to go downstairs when she appeared with the maid, carrying red lacquer trays. “We're having Cantonese raw fish today,” she announced with a smile. “It's my first attempt, so I don't know whether it will work. If it tastes bad, blame Gu for teaching me badly.” “It's your first time making it, and my first time seeing it. How does one eat it?” Hu went over to look. In the centre was an empty large platter of the sort used for shark's fin. Around it stood more than a dozen dishes of various sizes, holding raw fish, shredded radish squeezed quite dry, fried vermicelli, crisp fried dough strands, salt, sugar, sesame oil, pepper and other seasonings. One dish contained green threads sliced as fine as hair. He could not identify them. “Tangerine leaves, for flavour,” she said. “They have to be cut very fine. It took me a great deal of work.” Hu was surprised, and rather touched, that this ‘female Zhang Fei’, so bold and indifferent to details, could settle down to such painstaking work. “You've taken such trouble!” “Don't compliment me yet. Taste it first.” All four helped tip the ingredients into the large platter and mix them evenly. Hu took a mouthful with his chopsticks and found it had a distinctive flavour. “Bring the wine,” said You, who had been silent for some time. “We must drink Little Uncle's health properly today.” It was a thoroughly happy meal. Hu became everyone's target as the other three urged cup after cup upon him. Well on the way to drunkenness, he ate two bowls of raw-fish and jidi congee and felt warm all over. In high spirits, he said, “Brother Five, let's go out for a walk.”

“Where do you want to go?” “We'll decide as we walk.” They rose, and Gu followed. “Seventh Sister,” he said apologetically, “it's Hu's first day here. I ought to keep him company.” After listening to Hu's advice, she had changed her attitude—a change requiring no more than a turn of thought. She had once told herself: What is so remarkable about men? Settling disputes over tea or arguing a case was nothing special. Even a mountain of knives or a cauldron of boiling oil would not make her frown. Now she kept reminding herself: I am a woman, a daughter of a respectable family. I am to claim kinship with the Wangs and become a daughter of an official household. I must show a woman's manner and not let people call me a bandit woman behind my back. With such thoughts in mind, Gu's remark seemed likely to make her brother and Hu think that she could not bear to part with her future husband. She felt both shy and annoyed. “Little Uncle has come, so naturally you should accompany him. Why tell me? As though I watched your every move and kept you under such fierce control! How exasperating!” She gave him a sidelong glare. Her charm lay in looking equally lovely pleased or displeased. Even a hostile glance seemed affectionate, and what she said was reasonable. Gu accepted his scolding with a willing heart.

It was Hu who stopped him. He wanted to give them time together. With their affairs taking a favourable turn and their difficulties near resolution, they must have much to say to each other tenderly. But if he said so, even if Gu agreed to stay, she would refuse. He therefore found a reason of his own. “No need, Old Gu. Brother Five and I have a few things to discuss. You needn't accompany us.” “Then where will you be?” Gu asked hesitantly. “I'll come and find you later.” You turned to Hu. “Let's go and sit with Second Miss.”

Their meeting place arranged, You accompanied Hu on foot to Yiqing House. Second Miss had gone out to entertain at a banquet. A capable newly hired house attendant, A’qiao, welcomed them, conducted them into the main room, and sent a male attendant to hurry Second Miss back. “How shall we amuse ourselves?” You asked. “Invite people to drink, or play cards?” “No need for cards.” Hu found A’qiao fair, neat and pretty. Her soft Wu speech was even more authentic than Second Miss's, and he took a strong liking to her. He volunteered a proposal. “I'll provide a little excitement. Let's arrange a double-table party.” “How many guests have you invited, Mr Hu?” A’qiao asked. “A double-table party won't look right with too few.” Such a party did not necessarily require two actual tables. Her remark showed that she treated him as one of the household and wanted to save him expense. Hu was not yet familiar with the customs of courtesan society and did not know how to reply. You understood her intention, and guessed that Hu had no guests ready to invite. He spoke frankly. “Sister A’qiao is right. There's plenty of time for a special entertainment. Let's wait until Second Miss comes.” A’qiao agreed, and Hu had to let the matter rest. In the inner room, the two men reclined on a rosewood couch, an opium tray between them, talking while they waited. “This attendant A’qiao is rather good,” Hu said. “She must be nearly thirty?” “Well?” You laughed. “Shall I make a match for you?”

Hu smiled without answering, giving his tacit consent. He was about to say something when the curtain lifted and Second Miss appeared gracefully. Naturally, she greeted him with attentive inquiries. Gu arrived soon afterwards and insisted on playing host. Courtesan entertainment had its unwritten rules: one entertained at the establishment of one's own favourite, and going from a feast at one house to another was called ‘turning tables’. For the sake of business sociability, Gu had an established acquaintance, Seventh Miss of Hongying House, whose rooms were in the next lane. He invited Hu to dine there first, then return to Yiqing House for a late supper. “That isn't the rule,” Second Miss objected. “Naturally, you should dine here first and then move to Hongying House.” Hu agreed, but You had another plan. He waved his hand. “Let's do as Gu suggests and come back for supper. Little Uncle isn't returning to the silk warehouse. He'll borrow an empty bed here tonight.” In that case, it made sense to enjoy the courtesan banquet elsewhere and return to Yiqing House last. After supper, Hu could rest without moving again. Second Miss agreed. She planned to stay with You at their small separate house and leave her own rooms at Yiqing House for Hu.

They went together to Hongying House. As soon as they were seated, Gu called for paper and brush to write invitations. Hu, scarcely recovered from his journey and reluctant to face elaborate sociability, stopped him. “No, no. Let the three of us enjoy ourselves.” Instead, Gu wrote summonses for the entertainers. The first was for Second Miss. Holding his brush, he asked Hu, adopting a different form of address, “Little Uncle, whom shall we call? Fourth Miss of Meixiang House, as before?” “Business is poor,” Seventh Miss put in. “Fourth Miss left the profession at the last festival.” You decided for Hu. “Why don't you two become ‘brothers-in-law’? Call Ninth Miss to keep Little Uncle company.” “Ninth Miss?” Gu said. “She's a qingguan.” Ninth Miss of Hongying House was a qingguan, a young performer who entertained guests through her singing. Gu was reminding You that if Hu summoned her, he could only enjoy her performance. Hu, however, understood You's intention and quickly said, “A qingguan is just what I want.” The host deferred to his guest and sent out the summonses. One performer was upstairs and the other only a lane away, so no time was lost. By the time the table was laid, Second Miss and Ninth Miss had arrived, each accompanied by a musician carrying a huqin, ready to sing without theatrical costume as the men drank.

The table was spacious enough for the women to sit among the guests instead of behind them, as custom otherwise required. Hu drew Ninth Miss nearer for a look. Her fringe covered her forehead, and she still had a child's air. “How old are you?” “Fifteen.” Hu looked from Seventh Miss back to her. One had an oval face, the other a round one; their looks and expressions were wholly different. “Are you actual sisters?” Ninth Miss smiled without answering. Gu replied, “Where would so many actual sisters come from? But Seventh Miss can make decisions for her.” Hu understood, but had no intention of arranging anything further and let the matter drop. “Ninth Miss,” Gu said, “what will you sing?” “Whatever Mr Hu would like to hear.” “Oh!” Hu smiled. “It seems you have quite a repertoire.” “Indeed. Girls change greatly as they grow up, and she's still very young. As for her art, she's certain to do well.” “Thank you, Brother-in-Law.” Ninth Miss smiled, showing two dimples that made her look sweet. “She'll certainly grow more accomplished. Her talents are worth cultivating.” “She'll depend on your support, Mr Hu,” Seventh Miss answered. Then she quietly asked Gu where Hu was staying.

“Why do you ask?” Gu said with a smile. “Are you worried that Mr Hu hasn't arranged somewhere to stay?” “No ivory ever comes out of a dog's mouth!” Seventh Miss made a little fist and tapped him on the back. “Let me tell you...” She spoke so softly that the others could not make out her murmuring. You grew impatient. “Can't you save your private talk for the pillow? Drink! Drink!” Seeing that a guest was displeased, Seventh Miss hastily smiled and apologized. She took the wine pot herself to serve them and had her younger sister sing a popular tune. Only then did the table become lively. As soon as the song ended, another summons arrived for Ninth Miss. “Forgive me. Please come and see me later,” she said, rising to leave. The company immediately seemed subdued again. You was deeply displeased. “She hadn't even warmed her seat before moving on to another party. There's no pleasure in a banquet like this.” Naturally uneasy, Seventh Miss tried soothing words and apologies. You scarcely acknowledged her, while Hu could not be bothered to answer. The atmosphere became awkward. Unable to maintain her dignity, she reproached Gu for saying nothing in her support, as though he wanted to see her humiliated. “I haven't blamed you, and now you're blaming me!” Gu, too, was becoming angry. “Now, now,” Second Miss intervened. “For my sake, please. Seventh Sister would never deliberately neglect honoured guests.” As she spoke, she tugged at You.

You said nothing, but Hu felt thoroughly uncomfortable. “It's all my fault,” he said, raising his cup to Gu and You. “I'll drink a penalty cup.” What was the penalty for? Gu was about to ask when Hu gave him a look urging him to let the matter rest. This only made Gu more apologetic. After considering, he said to Second Miss, “Let's go to your place.” “How could I?” She looked troubled, out of loyalty to her fellow courtesan. “We're very comfortable here,” Hu said deliberately. “Seventh Miss, would you bring me a hot towel?” Once she had gone, he advised Gu and You not to take a passing entertainment so seriously. Neither answered, but Second Miss was deeply moved. He was so good-tempered and considerate, she said; what fortunate woman would have such a patron! This reminded You of something. He drew her aside and whispered in her ear. Her bright eyes kept glancing at Hu as she listened and nodded. At last she said, “Leave it to me.” “Did you hear?” You laughed. “Second Miss has it in hand.” Understanding, Hu returned a grateful smile. Gu did not understand, but their expressions suggested an amusing development, and one that certainly would not occur at Hongying House. He rose. “Let's go.” To leave like this would embarrass Seventh Miss, so both Hu and Second Miss persuaded him to stay. He sat down again at last, but their pleasure was nearly spent.

They endured until the clock struck ten, when the feast could finally end. Back at Second Miss's small separate house, they served no further wine. Over tea and quiet conversation, they found instead the pleasure of good friends gathered together. Hu told them about his experiences in Huzhou and Liu Bucai's amusing exploits. You simply found the stories entertaining; Gu saw a further significance. “This Mr Liu is a rare talent. Could he be brought to Shanghai?” “Certainly. Have you a use for him?” “Yes. He would make an excellent professional companion to guests. This ten-mile foreign settlement is full of extraordinary sights; it takes just such a man to find his way about. I'd like him to do nothing but entertain our visitors. Sons of great families, pampered young gentlemen and influential officials all like to see something of the foreign settlement. If someone can keep them amused, everything becomes easier to discuss.” His view was close to Hu's own. Hu readily agreed and decided to write for Liu the following day.

They went on to talk business at length. Gu had ideas for everything from opening a theatre to buying land, and explained them all persuasively. Yet every venture rested on Shanghai's future prosperity, and prosperity first required stability. Though the foreign settlement escaped the fighting, the Small Swords Society's occupation of the county town remained a danger close at hand. Meanwhile, the Jiangsu authorities were quietly contending with the foreigners and obstructing traders, which would seriously damage the settlement's market. Following this train of thought, Hu reached a new conclusion. “Old Gu, I think I'd better sell that consignment of silk soon.” “Why?” Gu asked attentively. “What's led you to that view?” “The ban on sending silk and tea to Shanghai cannot last long. If it continues, both sides will suffer. The foreigners will be in difficulty, certainly, but Shanghai's trade will also decline. We ought to mediate and remove the causes of their hostility, so that officials trust the foreigners and foreigners trust the officials. Only then can Shanghai flourish. At that point, whether we open a theatre or buy land, everything will prosper. Am I right?”

Gu and You nodded gravely. “Little Uncle, you've seen further,” Gu said with deep admiration. “That is how to do great business. Helping the authorities is helping ourselves. At present, both the governor-general's and the governor's yamens resent the British for supplying Liu Lichuan. They've reached something of a deadlock, almost a contest of temper. In fact, both sides regret it. The Chinese authorities, for instance, would at least lose customs revenue if they really cut off the foreign merchants' livelihood. The restrictions are a last resort. If someone mediated, a reconciliation would by no means be impossible. But when all is said and done, we're merely merchants. Foreigners respect merchants, so we can certainly make ourselves heard there. The difficulty is how to make contact with our own officials.” You spoke slowly. “There's one avenue we might try: Provincial Education Commissioner He.” “Exactly!” Gu agreed. “An excellent avenue. Though his work concerns the licentiate examinations, he often submits memorials on military affairs in Jiangsu. A meeting with him is sure to help.”

“Seeing him should be easy enough. But asking Prefect Wang for a letter of introduction will take some arranging.” Hu considered. “Then why don't you go yourself and deliver that letter from Prefect Wang in person? That would gain you a meeting.” If this undertaking succeeded, Gu's reputation would rise at once. Eager to try, he gladly accepted the suggestion. Yet rushing off with nothing but empty talk would serve no purpose. He must first contact the British consul, ascertain his intentions and judge whether agreement was possible. Only then could he act. This meant the matter would take more than two or three days. “The letter is urgent too,” Gu said, deciding to undertake an extra journey. “I'll go first, make Commissioner He's acquaintance and act as the opportunity offers. Meanwhile, please write to Prefect Wang for a letter recommending me, so we have it ready even if we don't need it.” “As you wish. Why not draft the recommendation yourself? I'll send it to Huzhou and ask him to copy it, affix his seal and return it. Wouldn't that save trouble?”

Full of enthusiasm, Gu was ready to take up his brush at once. You saw that it was past midnight and did not wish to spoil Hu's pleasant night. He stopped Gu, saying tomorrow would be soon enough. Then he and Second Miss accompanied Hu to his borrowed bed. “We've really neglected you today,” Gu said apologetically. “That dinner at Hongying House was thoroughly disappointing. Seventh Miss even wanted me to ask for your patronage. She has no sense of occasion.” “It doesn't matter,” Hu replied. “It's only a matter of spending a little money. I need somewhere to meet friends as well. I might as well become that young singer's patron.” “Forget it, Little Uncle,” You said. “I'd advise you to do as I do. It works very well.” Gu did not quite understand, but Hu did. If A’qiao pleased him, he might rent a small separate house too. Establishing a household in Huzhou had already strained his funds. Why bring another burden upon himself? With Second Miss present, however, he could not refuse openly. He merely put the matter off. “We'll see.”
